name: Tannat

lines.s10: Tannat is the dark red of Madiran in south west France and the national grape of Uruguay: blackberry, liquorice and a firm grip.
lines.s20: Tannat comes from Madiran, in the hills of Gascony, and few grapes carry more tannin. It is nearly black, with blackberry, black plum and liquorice, and Uruguay makes a rounder, softer version of it.
lines.s45: Tannat is a grape of real grip, nearly black and firmly tannic, at home in Madiran, in Gascony. It tastes of blackberry, black plum and cassis, with liquorice and a note of dark chocolate. It is full bodied and fresh, and its tannin dries the mouth as strong tea does. Madiran tames it with time in oak barrels and tiny doses of oxygen, while Uruguay's mild sea air usually gives a rounder, softer wine. It wants rich food: duck confit, cassoulet or a fatty grilled steak. A Basque settler planted it in Uruguay in the 1870s, and for generations the country called it by his name, Harriague.
lines.sale: Tannat came to Uruguay with a Basque settler and became the national grape: blackberry, liquorice and a firm, fresh grip. I would decant it first and pour it with the ribeye or the duck.

glass.lead: Blackberry, black plum and cassis with liquorice, smoke and dark chocolate, opaque and full, on very firm, drying tannin.

ladder.where: Madiran and Irouléguy in France; Canelones and Maldonado in Uruguay
Cafayate in Salta, northern Uruguay and Paso Robles

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, tannin very high and firm, alcohol medium plus, body full.

old.where: Madiran, Irouléguy and Saint-Mont in south west France
old.glass: Tends to be firmer and more savoury: blackberry, cassis and black plum with iron, leather, smoke and liquorice, fresh acidity and a wall of drying tannin when young. Time brings it round.
old.cellar: Tannat leads the blend, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Fer beside it; long soaks on the skins, oak, and often small doses of oxygen to soften the tannin.

new.where: Uruguay, in Canelones and Maldonado; Cafayate in Salta; Paso Robles in California
new.glass: Typically rounder and more fruit led: blackberry, black plum and blueberry with liquorice and dark chocolate, the tannin still firm but riper and finer. Maldonado's granite hills tend to give fresher wines than the clay of Canelones.
new.cellar: Bottled under the grape's name, alone or blended with Merlot or Cabernet Franc to soften it; some cellars use oak or small doses of oxygen, and rosé is made too.

contrast.why: Madiran keeps Tannat in the lead by law and soaks it long, so the wine is stern. Uruguay is humid and moderated by the sea, and climate and gentler handling give rounder tannin. France labels the place, Uruguay the grape.
contrast.blur: Modern Madiran, picked riper and softened with oxygen, can be supple when young, and the high desert of Cafayate gives Tannat as dark and tannic as Madiran's.
contrast.call: Iron, leather and a stern, drying grip lean Madiran; blueberry, riper fruit and rounder, finer tannin lean Uruguay.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: cool room temperature, since warmth makes the alcohol show.
service.decant: Consider it for a young wine after tasting a sample; an old Madiran may be decanted off its sediment.
service.age: Many Uruguayan wines are ready young; Madiran from a good year keeps ten years and more.

with.why: the Gascon match: beans, sausage and duck fat meet the grip

with.dish: Duck confit, duck breast or rack of lamb
with.why: fat and salt make firm tannin feel smoother

with.dish: Ribeye or beef from the grill
with.why: Uruguay's own table: charred, fatty beef and a firm red

with.dish: Hard sheep's milk cheese from the Pyrenees
with.why: salt and fat ease the tannin

labels.means: A red only appellation of Gascony, led by Tannat with the two Cabernets and Fer beside it.
The French Basque appellation: firm reds and rosés of Tannat and Cabernet Franc, from terraces near Spain.
The old name for Tannat in Uruguay, after the Basque settler who planted it.
A common Uruguayan blend: the Merlot rounds off the tannin.

guest.q: I have never heard of Tannat. What is it close to?
guest.a: Think of Cabernet Sauvignon with more colour and more grip, or a firmer, drier Malbec. It comes from Gascony in south west France, and Uruguay has made it its national red.

guest.q: Is the one from Uruguay different from the French?
guest.a: Usually rounder. Uruguay is humid and near the sea, and its Tannat tends to show riper fruit and finer tannin. Madiran is the sterner wine, and the one to keep.

guest.q: Will it soften if we give it time?
guest.a: Air can open the aroma within the hour, and years in the cellar soften the grip. Tonight the surest help is the food: fat and salt make the tannin feel smoother.

compare.tell: Malbec is plusher and softer, with a lift of violet; Tannat is firmer and drier, with higher acidity and far more tannin.
Sagrantino matches Tannat's grip but smells of black cherry preserve, dried violet and incense; Tannat is cassis, iron, leather and smoke.
Cabernet Sauvignon shows cedar and a leafy edge of green bell pepper; Tannat is darker and more tannic, with liquorice and iron.

cards.front: Tannat: its French home, and the grapes blended with it there?
cards.back: Madiran, in Gascony: red only and led by Tannat, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Fer beside it. Irouléguy and Saint-Mont grow it too.

cards.front: Tannat blind: Madiran or Uruguay, what tips it?
cards.back: Iron, leather and a stern, drying grip lean Madiran. Blueberry, riper fruit and rounder, finer tannin lean Uruguay.

cards.front: What method did Madiran develop in the early 1990s to soften Tannat?
cards.back: Micro-oxygenation: tiny, measured doses of oxygen fed into the wine in tank, to soften the tannin and fix the colour. It is now used far beyond Madiran.

questions.q: A blind red is opaque purple black, with blackberry, black plum and blueberry, liquorice and dark chocolate. The tannin is high but ripe and fine, and the fruit is generous. The table agrees it is Tannat. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Blueberry, generous fruit and rounder, finer tannin tend to mark Uruguay. Madiran and Irouléguy are typically sterner, with iron and leather, and Colchagua is known for Carmenère and Cabernet, not Tannat.

questions.q: A table orders a young Madiran with the duck breast, and one guest fears the wine will be too tannic for her. What is the sound thing to tell her?
opts: The duck's fat and salt will smooth the grip
Decanting will take the tannin out
Chilling it well will hide the tannin
Tannat loses its tannin once it is bottled
questions.exp: Fat and salt soften the impression of tannin, which is why Gascony pours Madiran with duck. Decanting can open the aroma but removes no tannin, and a cold tannic red feels harder, not softer.

questions.q: A guest sees Tannat Merlot beside a Uruguayan red on the list and asks why the two grapes are blended. What do you say?
opts: Merlot's soft fruit rounds off Tannat's firm tannin
Merlot adds the colour that Tannat lacks
Merlot raises the acidity of the blend
The law of Uruguay asks for a second grape
questions.exp: Tannat has colour, acidity and tannin to spare, so growers blend in Merlot to soften it. It is short of neither colour nor acidity, and Uruguay has no rule that asks for a second grape.

sources.title: INAO: cahier des charges of the appellation Madiran
Wine Enthusiast: Tannat, the dark prince of Paso Robles wine

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it and as TASTE.world, both, requires: Madiran, Irouléguy and Saint-Mont against Uruguay, with Cafayate and Paso Robles beside it.

The Codex says the grape two ways: tah-NAH on the South West France page and tah-NAHT on the Uruguay page. The entry gives both, the Uruguayan first, since that is the form a guest here is likelier to hear.

The Codex's records disagree with each other on two dials. The Régionale row gives Tannat high acidity and a warm climate; TASTE gives acidity medium plus and a moderate climate, and the profile reads acid medium to high. The entry follows TASTE and the profile: acidity medium plus, and a ladder of two rungs, moderate for Madiran and the coast of Uruguay, warm for Cafayate, northern Uruguay and Paso Robles.

No percentage is given for Tannat in Madiran. The sources read through search disagree (60 per cent of the vineyard in one, 60 to 80 per cent of the blend in another), the text of November 2025 could not be opened, and the Codex's own record says only that Tannat leads. The entry says the same. The lighter style the 2025 text is reported to admit, Bleu Tannat, is too new to teach and is left out.
Manseng Noir, which the Codex lists as an accessory grape in the text of November 2025, is left out of the blend named here for room; the two Cabernets and Fer stand in every text read.

The name is not explained. The sources read give two roots, the tan colour of the berry and the tannin, and call neither settled. Tannat day, 14 April, is left out: the sources read disagree on whether the date marks the birth or the death of Pascual Harriague. He died in 1894 and is named once, on a label line, where the grape's old name needs him.

For a century, of the name Harriague, stands on the Codex's Régionale bank; the Uruguay page says for decades. The 1870s stand on both; the sources read give 1870, 1871 and 1874 for the planting, so no year is given.

Cardamom stands beside liquorice on a widely repeated trade description of the grape, not on a regional body's; a checker may prefer liquorice with black pepper. Raspberry on the moderate rung is the young wine's note in the reference works.

Texas and Virginia also grow and bottle Tannat, on a general reference and on Virginia's wine body read through search; only Paso Robles is named, since four sources are the cap. The federal approval of the name, reported as 2002, could not be confirmed and is left out.
No Creole dish is given: none of the seven suits a wine this tannic.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after ten fixes over two rounds. Madiran and its blend, Irouléguy, Saint-Mont, Harriague and the 1870s, the granite of Maldonado and the clay of Canelones, and micro-oxygenation born in Madiran were confirmed; the call leaned on blueberry the notes did not carry, three tells parted Tannat from its neighbours by notes both carry, one label made Madiran the only red of Gascony, and the New World cellar called a method common that only some cellars use.
changed: lines.s45, the worlds clause: while Uruguay's mild sea air gives a rounder, softer wine now reads while Uruguay's mild sea air usually gives a rounder, softer wine. The Uruguay clause was said as a rule; usually hedges it.

glass.notes, spice: The call, a card and the worlds question lean on blueberry for Uruguay, as the reviewed profile does, but the notes carried none; a blue fruit group now holds it. Cardamom stood on one trade description alone, as the author reported, and cracked black pepper takes its place.

labels, Irouléguy: The French Basque appellation: firm, Tannat led reds and rosés from terraces near Spain now reads The French Basque appellation: firm reds and rosés of Tannat and Cabernet Franc, from terraces near Spain. Tannat led was looser than the rule: the cahier of 2024 makes Tannat and Cabernet Franc the two main grapes of the red, with Cabernet Sauvignon an accessory.
compare, the Malbec tell: The tell gave blueberry to Malbec as a parting note, and this entry lists blueberry among Tannat's own; the violet lift alone stays.

worlds.contrast.old.glass: Tends to be the firmer and more savoury now reads Tends to be firmer and more savoury. The firmer reads as the firmer of two wines not yet named; firmer, as the other side says riper.

lines.s45: and for a century the country called it by his name, Harriague now reads and for generations the country called it by his name, Harriague. For a century is the Régionale bank's and for decades the Uruguay record's; for generations holds both and claims neither figure.
labels, Madiran: The red appellation of Gascony reads as the only one, and Saint-Mont and Tursan are red too; a red only appellation is what the rule says.

compare, the Sagrantino tell: The tell gave cocoa to Sagrantino and blackberry to Tannat, and this entry lists dark chocolate and blackberry among Tannat's notes while the reviewed Sagrantino profile carries cocoa and blackberry too. Dried violet, from the Sagrantino profile, and cassis, iron and leather, which it does not carry, now part them.

compare, the Cabernet Sauvignon tell: The tell gave cassis to Cabernet as a parting note, and this entry lists cassis among Tannat's own; cedar and the green pepper edge, which Tannat lacks, part them.

worlds.contrast.new.cellar: oak and small doses of oxygen are common, and rosé is made too now reads some cellars use oak or small doses of oxygen, and rosé is made too. Oak and small doses of oxygen are common said more than the sources show: some Uruguayan wineries use micro-oxygenation and others argue it flattens the wine, and the trade reports a turn to less oak.
open: An explanation says Colchagua is known for Carmenère and Cabernet, not Tannat: true of a list, though Chile grows a little Tannat; left.
